You should try the following : check your connection, disable ad-blocker, clear your browser cache, try in private mode, try from another browser/computer/connection. 0 Hadrian's Wall When visiting the North of Britannia in 122 AD, the Roman Emperor Hadrian Augustus witnessed the aftermath of war between his armies and the savage Picts. In a show of Roman might, he ordered a wall to be built that would separate the Pict tribes from the rest of England. Grand in its design, the wall stretched 80 Roman miles, from coast to coast. Hadrian's Wall stood in service to the Roman Empire for nearly 300 years before its eventual decline. Today, Hadrian's Wall is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the remains of the forts, towers, and turrets can still be explored. In Hadrian's Wall, players take on the role of a Roman General placed in charge of the construction of a milecastle and bordering wall. Over six years (rounds), players will construct their fort and wall, man the defenses, and attract civilians by building services and providing entertainment - all while defending the honor of the Roman Empire from the warring Picts. The player who can accumulate the most renown, piety, valor and discipline, whilst avoiding disdain, will prove to the Emperor they are the model Roman citizen and be crowned Legatus Legionis! Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Start of Year 3 Turns 3.1 Advice 4 Left Board Tracks 5 Cohorts 6 Mining and Foresting 7 Wall Guard 8 Cippi / Wall / Fort 9 Granaries 10 Resource Production 11 Training Ground 12 Hotels / Workshops / Roads 13 Forum 14 Landmarks 15 Attributes 16 Right Board Tracks 17 Citizens 18 Precincts 19 Market 20 Theatre 21 Ludus Gladiatorius 22 Gardens 23 Temples 24 Baths 25 Courthouse 26 Diplomats 27 Scouts 28 End of Year 29 End of Game Overview The game is played over 6 years (rounds) where players take actions until everyone passes and then any unused Workers and Resources are discarded to the general supply, each Year concludes with an attack from the Picts and you must try to defend yourself! Start of Year Turn over a new Fate Card and everyone gains the resources listed Each player draws 2 personal cards and chooses one for a Path and the other for a Prospect The Path option looks at the top "sky" part of the card which will suggest an objective which will grant extra points if achieved The Prospect option looks at the lower left tag which will provide additional starting supplies After this decision has been made, players gain extra supplies based on what they have filled in so far: 1 Resource per filled space in Resource Production 1 Civilian per filled space in Hotel 1 Builder per filled space in Workshop 1 Attribute per filled space in Road Turns Advice Due to difficulties with implementing an effective undo system, it is advised that players plan their entire go BEFORE picking their Path Card, perhaps as an Excel Spreadsheet (beginning with starting supplies, subtracting supplies for costs and adding supplies for bonuses, don't forget to track chain bonuses e.g. if you get to advance on another track which also gives a bonus) until you're happy that you've spent your supplies effectively and end the turn with minimal wastage Please note that if you intend to use the above system, extra supplies are distributed AFTER Path selection, and as such the supplies it says you have may not be all you have to use that turn The main phase allows players to use their supplies to take actions which involve filling in spaces from left to right on various tracks and perhaps gaining extra supplies if the space filled contained an icon The cost to advance on a track is shown in the banner where that track's name can be found Some areas work slightly differently, maybe filling in a different direction or being filled in whatever order you like If a space has a "#" icon, it is filled with the year number rather than shaded in There are 22 different action area types, some of which having multiple different sub-tracks within them These are split into Besides, this something is full of abstract and absurd elements following recently popular designers trend: „I’ll put in as much elements as possible and will pretend that all this fits together in a way that only elite geeks can appreciate”. [Rating: 1/10] Played only once and no desire to ever play again - at three players it was the most tedious gaming experience I've ever had.

[Rating: 1/10] Does little to turn me into a proponent of roll/draw & write games. Showed some promise early, lots of options, seemed flexible, many paths to choose. But every time I've played thus far, the game turns into a total slog by the the halfway mark and before long I'm just praying for it to end. Struggling to suss out exactly why it can't hold my attention for a full playthrough. Maybe there's [i]too[/i] much going on, considering the genre is generally built upon simpler, more whimsical fundamentals. Or maybe I'm experiencing fatigue for these relentless resource conversion-type games. (After all

[Rating: 1/10] Neat blend of a roll & write with a resource conversion euro, the "do x to do y to do z" resource conversion puzzle mixed with the classic roll & write "moving up this track moves me up on this other one which etc" dopamine hits is really entertaining. That said, I do question the replayability as regardless of what resources you gain from the flop each round there seems to be certain tracks that more readily yield bonuses for the early game while others are clearly late game resource dumps for points so I suspect the strategy will be samey with more plays. Also, it feels like a solo-only game

[Rating: 1/10] A roll & write with a billion areas on the board. Not the worst I've played, but also it felt like tedious building.

[Rating: 1/10] This game accurately produces the fun one obtains when filling out tax forms.  Seriously, the game amounts to filling in boxes on a sheet of paper, which then means you get to jump to other portions of the form and follow the rules to fill out that section.  It has taken me a long time and hundreds of games to finally find a game worse than Monopoly.  This is it.

[Rating: 2/10] This is a great option for playing during a lockdown. The gameplay feels designed to be unsociable, with players largely doing their own thing until each finishes, and then communally facing the same attack patterns at different mileposts. Is it engaging as solitaire? Sure. But there is no reason to play with more people than than unless all else is exhausted.

[Rating: 2/10] Like paying 'Accounting - The Game'. Just a lot of bookkeeping and very little game.

[Rating: 2/10] Perhaps one of the worst games I have ever played.  Does this game function? Yes Does it look good? Yes  But, it's the exact same every time you play it. You'll always see all of your cards every game. You'll always have to build most things in a certain order every game. You'll always have to gamble against getting attacked each turn.  The stunning appearance of variety hides how truly shallow Hadrian's Wall is

[Rating: 2.351/10] I just dislike this game so much - it basically like doing your taxes.  More a puzzle than a game with zero player interaction and it all seems pointless.  One of the few games I would push against playing again. Rating 2.351,  June 2023)

[Rating: 2.5/10] Too complicated for a roll and write! Then again, I kinda want to try it again...

[Rating: 3/10] I was pretty disappointed in Hadrian's Wall. There were a lot of things that I didn't like. The biggest was that the game was extremely overwhelming and lent itself to some serious AP. I dreaded gaining new workers because I wanted the rounds to end already and not have to continue searching the best places to use them. The end game objectives are completely boring also. 1/2/3 VP in a game that has scores upwards of 70. I never felt incentivized to push for the higher VP tier. Also don't expect to have fun with anyone at the table, this is a very silent, solitaire puzzle, which is fine sometim

[Rating: 3/10] There's way too much going on in this flip-n-write that I don't think it's worth the effort to learn. If you like resource management and min/maxing points by yourself, this is a game for you. But it takes a while to play, and while I'm fine with some multiplayer solitaire games, they can't both take a long time and be centered around filling out a worksheet. One or the other please. If a game is mostly crossing boxes, it should be more on the Ganz Schon Clever side (short and simple) rather than the heavy euro side.
